lessons.title: Implementing Markov Switching Models in Python with statsmodels

body.text: statsmodels turns the last two lessons' equations into a single .fit() call. Reading its output correctly, filtered versus smoothed versus decoded, matters just as much as running it.

children.text: Lesson 1 defined Markov switching regression conceptually. Lesson 2 applied it to volatility persistence through a log realized variance proxy. This lesson fits both in Python using statsmodels.tsa.regime_switching, the library most practitioners reach for outside of hmmlearn.

cells: Regime-dependent mean and variance, no autoregressive term on the series itself
Regime-dependent mean, variance, and autoregressive coefficients

children.text: Fitting MarkovAutoregression on a Nifty Volatility Proxy

body.code:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.regime_switching.markov_autoregression import MarkovAutoregression

log_rv = np.log(nifty_df['realized_vol_20d']).dropna()

ms_model = MarkovAutoregression(
    log_rv,
    k_regimes=2,
    order=1,
    switching_ar=True,
    switching_variance=True,
)

ms_result = ms_model.fit(search_reps=20)
print(ms_result.summary())
body.caption: Fitting a 2-regime Markov switching autoregression on log realized volatility, with 20 randomized starting-value searches

children.text: k_regimes sets the number of hidden states, order sets how many lags the autoregression uses, and switching_ar and switching_variance control which coefficients are allowed to differ by regime, exactly the design choice from Lesson 1's scenario exercise. The summary output labels regime-specific parameters by index, typically entries like const[0] and const[1] for the regime-specific intercepts, and p[0->0], p[1->0] for transition probabilities; inspect ms_result.params directly to see the exact labels for your fitted model.

body.text: This fit is subject to the exact same local-optimum risk as hmmlearn's Baum-Welch in Chapter 3. search_reps=20 tells statsmodels to try 20 randomized starting points and keep the best one, the statsmodels equivalent of Chapter 3's multi-seed loop. Skipping this on a single default fit risks landing on a poor local optimum without any warning that it happened.

children.text: Reading the Fitted Output: Filtered vs Smoothed vs Decoded

body.code:
filtered_probs = ms_result.filtered_marginal_probabilities
smoothed_probs = ms_result.smoothed_marginal_probabilities

print(filtered_probs.tail())
print(smoothed_probs.tail())
body.caption: Two different regime-probability outputs from the same fitted model

children.text: These are genuinely different quantities, not two names for the same thing. filtered_marginal_probabilities uses only data up to and including each day, matching the filtering concept from Chapter 2 and 3. smoothed_marginal_probabilities uses the entire sample, running forward-backward across all the data, so it can revise an earlier day's probability using later evidence, the same principle behind Chapter 3's Viterbi reversal example. It is not, however, the same thing as a Viterbi decode: smoothed probabilities give a continuous probability for each state at each time, while Viterbi commits to a single most likely state sequence. Use filtered for anything resembling a live decision, and smoothed or Viterbi-decoded labels for historical analysis and backtesting.
Expected Regime Durations, Straight From the Fit

body.caption: Expected duration per regime, computed automatically from the fitted transition matrix

body.text: This single line computes exactly Chapter 1's E[duration] = 1 / (1 - p) formula, and exactly Chapter 3's self-transition intuition, but on real, fitted Nifty data instead of illustrative numbers. If the calm regime's expected duration comes back at a few days instead of a few weeks, that is a strong signal something is off in the fit, the number of regimes, the proxy series, or the search_reps setting, before you trust anything else the model tells you.

body.title: Fit and Inspect Your Own Markov Switching Model
steps: Compute a volatility proxy, such as log(realized_vol_20d), from Chapter 2's rolling realized volatility, and drop NaN values
Fit a MarkovAutoregression with k_regimes=2, order=1, switching_ar=True, switching_variance=True, using fit(search_reps=20)
Inspect ms_result.params and identify which regime has the higher fitted variance; that is your Stressed state
Print ms_result.expected_durations and compare it against Chapter 1's illustrative persistence ranges
Plot filtered_marginal_probabilities against the Nifty price chart and visually check that the higher-variance regime's probability rises during known stress periods like 2020 and 2022

body.title: Choosing the Right Probability Output
body.question: Which output should you use to build a live, day-by-day trading signal, and why?
options: smoothed_marginal_probabilities, because it uses the most data available
filtered_marginal_probabilities, because it only uses data available up to each day, matching what you would actually know while trading live
The Viterbi-decoded path, because it commits to a single, confident answer
It does not matter which output you use; all three produce identical numbers
body.explanation: Both smoothed_marginal_probabilities and a Viterbi decode use the entire sample, including data from after the day in question, which makes them look-ahead-biased if used for a live decision. Only filtered_marginal_probabilities respects the information actually available at each point in time, which is exactly what a live trading signal must do.

points: MarkovRegression matches Chapter 3's HMM (regime-dependent mean and variance only); MarkovAutoregression adds regime-dependent autoregressive coefficients as in Lesson 1
search_reps in .fit() runs multiple randomized starting points and keeps the best, the statsmodels equivalent of Chapter 3's multi-seed hmmlearn fitting
filtered_marginal_probabilities uses only data up to each day; smoothed_marginal_probabilities uses the full sample and can revise earlier estimates
Smoothed probabilities and a Viterbi decode are related but distinct: smoothed gives a continuous probability per state per day, Viterbi commits to one specific state sequence
ms_result.expected_durations computes Chapter 1's E[duration] = 1/(1-p) formula directly from the fitted model, and is a fast, meaningful sanity check on any fit
Live decisions must use filtered probabilities only; smoothed probabilities and Viterbi decodes are for historical analysis and backtesting, where using future information is not a look-ahead problem
